data:
[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = [
    "crates/xerj-server",
    "crates/xerj-common",
    "crates/xerj-storage",
    "crates/xerj-fts",
    "crates/xerj-vector",
    "crates/xerj-logs",
    "crates/xerj-query",
    "crates/xerj-rerank",
    "crates/xerj-api",
    "crates/xerj-ai",
    "crates/xerj-compress",
    "crates/xerj-engine",
    "crates/xerj-mcp",
    "crates/xerj-wasm",
    "crates/xerj-cluster",
    "crates/xerj-console-api",
    "crates/xerj-autoindex",
    "crates/xerj-hub",
    "crates/xerj-sources",
    "tests/es-compat-yaml",
]

[workspace.package]
version = "1.0.0-rc.102"
edition = "2021"
license = "Apache-2.0"
authors = ["xerj Contributors"]

[workspace.dependencies]
# Async runtime
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
# HTTP
axum = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros"] }
# `h2` is the HTTP/2 implementation under every listener (hyper for REST +
# ES-compat, tonic for gRPC) and under `reqwest` on the client side. Nothing in
# this workspace calls it directly outside the `xerj-server` regression test,
# but the floor is declared here on purpose: 0.4.16-0.4.18 size the small-DATA-
# frame budget (the RUSTSEC-2026-0258 mitigation) at a fixed 25,600 bytes,
# which a legitimate authenticated request chunked below ~200 bytes exhausts —
# the client is answered `GOAWAY ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` (#485). 0.4.19 scales the
# budget with the configured connection window instead (half of it, floor
# 25,600), so hyper's 1 MiB server window yields 512 KiB of headroom while the
# empty-DATA-frame vector the advisory was filed for stays capped at 100 frames
# by a separate counter. Declaring the floor here means `cargo update` cannot
# resolve back to a version with the fixed budget.
h2 = "0.4.19"
tower = "0.4"
tower-http = { version = "0.5", features = ["cors", "trace", "limit", "decompression-gzip"] }
# Serialization
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = { version = "1", features = ["raw_value"] }
simd-json = "0.14"
# SIMD-accelerated byte search
memchr = "2"
# Config
toml = "0.8"
# Logging
tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter", "json"] }
# Parallel compute
rayon = "1.10"
# Concurrent data structures
dashmap = "6"
arc-swap = "1"
crossbeam = "0.8"
# Data structures
roaring = "0.10"
fst = "0.4"
bitpacking = "0.9"
# Compression
lz4_flex = "0.11"
zstd = "0.14.3"
# Hashing
xxhash-rust = { version = "0.8", features = ["xxh3"] }
rustc-hash = "2"
crc32fast = "1"
# Crypto/Random
rand = "0.8"
# ed25519 pack signatures (harvest/sign.rs); same crate the TLS stack uses,
# so it adds no new native build to the binary.
ring = "0.17"
# Bytes
bytes = "1"
memmap2 = "0.9"
byteorder = "1"
# Error handling
thiserror = "2"
anyhow = "1"
# Time
chrono = { version = "0.4", features = ["serde"] }
# UUID
uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v4", "serde"] }
# S3 / S3-compatible object storage (Cloudflare R2, MinIO, AWS S3, ...).
#
# `default-features = false` is load-bearing, not tidiness. The default
# feature set routes through `aws-smithy-runtime/default-https-client`, which
# selects `aws-smithy-http-client/rustls-aws-lc` — i.e. aws-lc-rs, a C/asm
# build. That is precisely the crypto backend the `tonic` line below
# deliberately keeps out of this tree because it breaks the musl/aarch64/
# windows cross-compile matrix. We instead pick the TLS stack explicitly via
# `aws-smithy-http-client` with `rustls-ring`, which reuses the rustls+ring
# already pulled in by `reqwest`/axum-server: hyper 1.x, no new C toolchain
# requirement, no second TLS implementation in the binary.
#
# `sigv4a` is also dropped from the default set: it only signs requests to
# S3 multi-region access points, which XERJ does not address. Plain SigV4 is
# what R2, MinIO and single-region S3 buckets accept.
aws-sdk-s3 = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = [
    "rt-tokio",
    "http-1x",
    "behavior-version-latest",
] }
# The HTTP client is supplied explicitly (see above). `rustls-ring` implies
# `__rustls` + `default-client` => hyper 1.x + hyper-rustls + tokio-rustls on
# the ring provider.
aws-smithy-http-client = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = [
    "rustls-ring",
] }
# TLS
rustls = "0.23"
rcgen = "0.13"
# Metrics. `default-features = false` drops the optional `protobuf` feature,
# which is the ONLY thing that pulled protobuf 2.28.0 into the tree
# (GHSA-2gh3-rmm4-6rq5, uncontrolled recursion when PARSING protobuf). We only
# ever ENCODE, and only to the text exposition format: `TextEncoder`, `Encoder`
# and `proto::MetricFamily` are all available without the feature (`proto` is
# then backed by prometheus's pure-Rust `src/plain_model.rs`). Only
# `ProtobufEncoder`/`PROTOBUF_FORMAT` are gated off, and nothing here uses them.
# Removing the dependency beats upgrading it — there is no protobuf parser left
# to be recursed into. Same reasoning as the `tonic` line below.
prometheus = { version = "0.13", default-features = false }
# gRPC (XerjSearch service on :8081). Default features only — the `tls`
# feature is intentionally OFF so tonic pulls no crypto backend (no
# aws-lc-rs / vendored OpenSSL); the gRPC listener speaks plaintext h2c,
# while the REST/ES listeners keep terminating TLS via axum-server+ring.
tonic = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["channel", "codegen", "prost", "router", "server"] }
prost = "0.13"
# Build-time codegen. `protox` is a PURE-RUST protobuf compiler, so the
# build needs NO `protoc` binary on the host — critical for the
# cross-compile matrix (musl/aarch64/windows/macos) where a host protoc
# is not guaranteed. It emits a FileDescriptorSet that tonic-build turns
# into Rust via `compile_fds` (never shelling out to protoc).
tonic-build = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["prost", "transport"] }
protox = "0.7"
# HTTP client (embedding proxy, hub, feedback). `rustls-tls-native-roots`
# adds the OS certificate store on top of the bundled Mozilla roots, so
# machines behind a TLS-inspecting proxy or antivirus (whose CA lives only
# in the OS store) can still reach hub.xerj.org instead of failing with
# rustls `UnknownIssuer` (#2746). Both root sets are loaded additively.
reqwest = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["json", "rustls-tls", "rustls-tls-native-roots", "http2", "charset"] }
# Testing
tempfile = "3"
# Benchmarking
criterion = { version = "0.5", features = ["html_reports"] }
# AST parsing. Only tree-sitter CORE is hoisted here: it declares
# `links = "tree-sitter"`, so two crates pinning different core versions is a
# hard resolution failure that takes out the whole workspace at once, not a
# duplicate-dep warning (#352: #327 pinned 0.25, #317 moved to 0.26, and the
# merge stopped resolving). One pin, one version. Per-crate grammar pins stay
# local; the `workspace-resolves` CI gate catches any links crate that drifts.
tree-sitter = "0.26"

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
strip = true
panic = "abort"

# CI test profile. Identical *code semantics* to [profile.release] --
# opt-level 3, debug-assertions off, overflow-checks off -- so tests still
# exercise optimized codegen. Only the optimization *scope* changes: no
# whole-program LTO and 16 codegen units instead of 1.
#
# Why it exists: `cargo test --release` links every one of the ~99 test
# binaries with fat LTO + codegen-units=1. On CI run 31571998506 that was
# 76m05s of compilation for 1m52s of actual test execution. `panic = "abort"`
# additionally forces cargo to rebuild the entire dependency graph with
# `panic = "unwind"` for test targets, so a preceding `cargo build --release`
# shares almost nothing with it; `panic = "unwind"` here makes that split
# explicit rather than accidental.
#
# [profile.release] above is deliberately untouched: release.yml builds the
# shipped binary with `cargo build --release`, and it must stay fat-LTO.
[profile.ci-test]
inherits = "release"
lto = false
codegen-units = 16
panic = "unwind"
strip = false

# Fast iteration profile: symbolized with thin LTO and parallel codegen.
# It is intentionally not production-codegen-equivalent.
# Fast verification profile — the BUILD half of the implement -> build -> verify
# loop. Its sibling is [profile.ci-test] above, which serves the TEST half.
#
# The division is deliberate and the two are not redundant:
#   quick    — `cargo build`. Inherits panic = "abort" from release, matching the
#              shipped binary, so the artifact you smoke-test behaves like the real
#              one (panic strategy is observable).
#   ci-test  — `cargo test`. Uses panic = "unwind", because cargo rebuilds the whole
#              dependency graph with unwind for test targets regardless; declaring it
#              makes that split explicit instead of accidental, and lets test builds
#              share artifacts with each other rather than fighting a build profile
#              they can never reuse.
#
# Use ci-test for `cargo test`. Use quick for `cargo build`. Neither is ever valid
# for a released artifact or a published number.
#
# WHY: [profile.release] below is a SHIPPING configuration — `lto = "fat"` plus
# `codegen-units = 1` is the slowest build Rust can produce, deliberately, because
# it yields the fastest binary. Fat LTO is a whole-program optimisation that runs
# largely single-threaded at link time, and codegen-units = 1 removes intra-crate
# parallelism, so a 32-core machine ends up watching one core. That is the right
# trade for an artifact users download and run for months. It is the wrong trade
# for an agent rebuilding to check whether a one-line fix compiles: the same cost
# is paid on every iteration, and the resulting binary's runtime speed is
# irrelevant to the question being asked.
#
# `quick` keeps everything that affects CORRECTNESS identical to release —
# panic = "abort" (inherited, and it changes observable behaviour, so it must
# match), the same feature set, the same target-cpu from .cargo/config.toml — and
# relaxes only what affects optimisation. A binary built with `quick` is a valid
# functional test of a release binary; it is NOT valid for measuring performance.
#
# USE IT FOR: does it compile, do the tests pass, does the ES-YAML suite stay at
#             0 failed, does this fix actually fix the bug.
# NEVER USE IT FOR: benchmarks, latency numbers, published measurements, or any
#             artifact that leaves this machine. Those must be --release.
#
#   cargo build --profile quick -p xerj-server
#   cargo test  --profile quick -p xerj-autoindex
#
[profile.quick]
inherits = "release"
lto = false          # the single biggest lever: no whole-program link-time pass
codegen-units = 16   # let 32 cores actually participate
opt-level = 2        # enough that tests are not pathologically slow
debug = false        # debuginfo is a large share of both build time and disk
strip = true
incremental = true   # meaningful for the edit-rebuild-edit loop this profile serves

[profile.profiling]
inherits = "release"
debug = 1
strip = false
lto = "thin"
codegen-units = 16

# Final confirmation profile: identical optimizer/LTO/codegen settings to
# release, but retains symbols for pprof.
[profile.profiling-final]
inherits = "release"
debug = 1
strip = false
